2-5.title: Weather vs Climate!
2-5.description: Learn the difference between today's weather and the usual weather where you live!

en.title: Weather vs Climate!
en.welcome: Hi little weather watcher! Weather is what's happening outside today, but climate is what the weather is usually like where you live. Let's explore!
en.mainContent:
Weather is what you see when you look outside right now. Is it sunny? Rainy? Snowy? Windy? That's today's weather! Weather changes every day and sometimes even during the same day.

Climate is the usual weather that happens where you live. If you live somewhere hot most of the time, that's your climate. If you live somewhere with snowy winters and warm summers, that's your climate. Climate is the pattern of weather over a long time!

Different places have different climates. Some places are hot all year (like deserts and tropical forests). Some places are cold all year (like the North and South Poles). Some places have seasons - hot summers, cold winters, and medium spring and fall.

Climate affects what can grow. In hot, rainy places, big trees and lots of plants grow (like rainforests). In cold places, only tough plants that can handle ice and snow grow. In deserts where it's very dry, only special plants that don't need much water can live.

Animals live in climates that are right for them. Polar bears live where it's cold and icy. Monkeys live where it's warm. Camels live in hot, dry deserts. Each animal is built for its climate!

People dress differently depending on climate. In cold climates, people wear warm coats, hats, and boots. In hot climates, people wear light, cool clothes. Houses are built differently too - some have thick walls to keep heat in, others have lots of windows to let breeze through.

Climate is changing a bit. The Earth is getting warmer overall. This makes ice at the North and South Poles melt a little. It changes when and where rain falls. Scientists are studying this to understand how to help Earth stay healthy.

You can help! Turning off lights when you leave a room, not wasting water, and taking care of trees all help Earth's climate stay healthy!
keyPoints: Weather is what's happening outside today; climate is usual weather patterns
Different places have different climates - hot, cold, or seasonal
Climate affects what plants and animals can live in each place
People adapt their clothes and homes to their climate
Earth's climate is changing and we can help keep it healthy
interactionPrompts: What's the weather like today where you are?
What's the climate usually like where you live?
en.wisdomMoment: Weather changes day to day, but climate is the big picture of what weather is usually like. Taking care of Earth helps keep the climate healthy for all living things!
en.core_metaphor: Weather is what clothes you wear today; climate is what clothes you have in your closet

abstract_concepts.climate: Usual weather patterns over a long time

en.cta: Notice the weather today, and think about what it's usually like where you live. That's climate!
en.summary: You've learned that weather is today's conditions while climate is long-term patterns, different places have different climates, climate affects plants and animals, people adapt to their climate, and Earth's climate is changing. Taking care of Earth helps!

6-12.title: Climate Zones and Global Patterns
6-12.description: Understand Earth's climate zones and atmospheric circulation

en.title: Climate Zones and Global Patterns
en.welcome: Hey young climatologist! Earth has distinct climate zones driven by sunlight distribution and atmospheric circulation. Understanding these patterns explains why different regions have different weather. Let's explore!
en.mainContent:
**Climate vs Weather**: Weather is atmospheric conditions at specific time and place (today's rain, this week's heat wave). Climate is average weather patterns over 30+ years (Mediterranean summers are hot and dry; Seattle winters are cool and wet). Climate describes what to expect; weather is what you get.

**Climate zones** result from Earth's spherical shape and tilted axis. Equatorial regions receive direct sunlight year-round (hot climates). Polar regions receive angled sunlight (cold climates). Temperate zones between them have seasons as Earth's tilt causes varying sun angles throughout the year. This creates major climate zones: tropical, subtropical, temperate, and polar.

**Tropical climates** near the equator are hot year-round with consistent day length (~12 hours). **Tropical rainforests** receive heavy rainfall creating lush vegetation (Amazon, Congo, Southeast Asia). **Tropical savannas** have wet and dry seasons supporting grasslands with scattered trees (African savannas). High biodiversity characterizes tropical zones due to consistent warmth and moisture.

**Desert climates** occur in subtropics and rain shadows. Descending air from atmospheric circulation creates high-pressure zones where air warms and dries (Sahara, Arabian, Australian deserts). Rain shadow deserts form on leeward sides of mountains where air has dropped moisture (Mojave behind Sierra Nevada). Deserts have extreme temperature swings - hot days, cold nights due to lack of moisture regulating temperature.

**Temperate climates** have distinct seasons from Earth's axial tilt. **Mediterranean** climates have wet winters and dry summers (California, Mediterranean coast, parts of Australia). **Humid continental** climates have cold winters and warm summers with year-round precipitation (US Midwest, Central Europe). **Marine west coast** climates have mild temperatures and frequent rain from ocean influence (Pacific Northwest, UK).

**Polar climates** have long, cold winters and short, cool summers. **Tundra** has permafrost (permanently frozen ground) with low-growing vegetation adapted to harsh conditions. **Ice caps** (Antarctica, Greenland) are permanently covered in ice with minimal precipitation - technically deserts due to low moisture.

**Atmospheric circulation** drives climate patterns. Hadley cells near the equator: rising warm air creates low pressure and rain; descending air at 30° latitude creates subtropical deserts. Ferrel cells in mid-latitudes and polar cells complete global circulation. Trade winds, westerlies, and polar easterlies result from these circulation patterns combined with Coriolis effect from Earth's rotation.

**Ocean currents** affect coastal climates. Warm currents (Gulf Stream) moderate temperatures, making Western Europe warmer than similar latitudes. Cold currents (Humboldt) cool coastal areas and reduce precipitation. El Niño and La Niña are Pacific Ocean temperature oscillations affecting global weather patterns - demonstrating ocean-atmosphere connections.

**Climate change** is altering these patterns. Global average temperature has risen 1.1°C since pre-industrial times. This shifts climate zones poleward, intensifies some weather extremes, changes precipitation patterns, and melts polar ice. Understanding climate science helps evaluate evidence and policy discussions.
keyPoints: Climate is 30+ year average patterns; weather is day-to-day conditions
Climate zones result from Earth's shape, tilt, and sunlight distribution
Atmospheric circulation (Hadley, Ferrel, polar cells) drives global patterns
Ocean currents moderate coastal climates and affect global weather
Climate change is shifting zones and intensifying extremes
interactionPrompts: What climate zone do you live in?

en.wisdomMoment: Climate zones demonstrate how Earth's physical properties (shape, tilt, rotation) create organized patterns from chaotic atmospheric processes. Understanding these patterns helps explain why each region has characteristic weather and ecosystems!
en.core_metaphor: Climate is like the script for a play; weather is the actual performance with improvisation
en.cta: Research your local climate zone. What are its defining characteristics? How do they affect ecosystems and human activities?
en.summary: You've learned climate vs weather distinction, climate zones from Earth's geometry, tropical climates with rainforests and savannas, deserts from atmospheric circulation and rain shadows, temperate zones with seasons, polar climates with tundra and ice, atmospheric circulation cells driving patterns, ocean currents affecting coastal climates, and climate change shifting zones. Climate patterns are predictable yet changing!

13-17.title: Climate Science and Change
13-17.description: Understand climate data, models, and anthropogenic climate change

en.title: Climate Science and Change
en.welcome: Climate science combines physics, chemistry, biology, and data analysis to understand Earth's climate system. Current climate change is the most significant environmental challenge facing humanity. Let's explore the science!
en.mainContent:
**Climate data** comes from multiple sources: weather station records (temperature, precipitation, pressure), satellite observations (ice extent, sea level, vegetation), ice cores (atmospheric composition over 800,000 years), tree rings (rainfall and temperature), ocean buoys and ships, and coral growth patterns. This multi-proxy approach builds comprehensive climate history.

**Greenhouse effect** is natural and essential. Atmospheric gases (water vapor, CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide) absorb infrared radiation Earth emits, warming the atmosphere. Without greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be -18°C instead of 15°C. The problem isn't the effect itself but its intensification from increased greenhouse gas concentrations.

**Carbon cycle**: CO₂ moves between atmosphere, oceans, biosphere, and geosphere. Photosynthesis removes atmospheric CO₂; respiration and decomposition release it. Oceans absorb CO₂, forming carbonic acid (causing ocean acidification). Volcanic outgassing adds CO₂ slowly; rock weathering removes it slowly. These natural flows were balanced until human activity disrupted equilibrium.

**Fossil fuel combustion** adds ~10 gigatons of CO₂ annually - taking carbon stored underground for millions of years and releasing it rapidly. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from 280 ppm (pre-industrial) to 420 ppm (current) - 50% increase. Isotope analysis proves this CO₂ is from fossil fuels (depleted in C-14). Deforestation contributes another ~1-2 gigatons annually by reducing carbon sinks.

**Climate models** simulate Earth's climate using physics equations (fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, radiative transfer) on supercomputers. Models divide atmosphere and oceans into grid cells, calculating interactions. Multiple models from institutions worldwide show consistent warming trends. Models successfully reproduce historical climate and predict observed changes, building confidence in future projections.

**Evidence for warming**: Global average temperature risen 1.1°C since 1850. Arctic sea ice declining. Glaciers retreating worldwide. Sea level rising 3.3 mm/year from thermal expansion and ice melt. Ocean heat content increasing. Spring arriving earlier. Species ranges shifting poleward. Multiple independent lines converge on same conclusion: Earth is warming.

**Attribution studies** calculate human contribution to observed warming. Using physics, models estimate natural climate factors (solar, volcanic) would have caused slight cooling. Observed warming matches greenhouse gas increases. Conclusion: observed warming is primarily human-caused (95%+ confidence).

**Projected impacts**: Without mitigation, global temperatures could rise 2-4°C by 2100. This shifts climate zones, intensifies heat waves and heavy precipitation, increases drought in some regions, raises sea levels, acidifies oceans, disrupts ecosystems, affects agriculture, and increases climate refugee numbers. Earlier and stronger action limits warming and impacts.

**Solutions** include: transitioning to renewable energy (solar, wind, nuclear), improving energy efficiency, electrifying transportation, carbon pricing, protecting and restoring forests, developing carbon capture technology, and adapting to unavoidable changes. Individual, corporate, and government action all necessary. Climate science informs policy but doesn't dictate it - values and priorities shape responses.
keyPoints: Climate data from multiple sources builds comprehensive understanding
Enhanced greenhouse effect from increased CO₂ drives observed warming
Fossil fuel combustion disrupted balanced carbon cycle adding 10+ gigatons CO₂ annually

Attribution studies show observed warming is primarily human-caused with high confidence

en.wisdomMoment: Climate science represents centuries of observation, experimentation, and theory-building across multiple disciplines. The scientific consensus on human-caused climate change is based on overwhelming evidence from independent sources. Understanding this science equips you to evaluate claims and participate in society's response!
en.core_metaphor: Earth's climate is like a bathtub filling faster than it drains - we control the faucet through our choices
en.cta: Research climate policies in your region. What actions are being taken? What gaps remain? How can you contribute?

Climate science is robust and urgent!

18-35.title: Climate Action and Your Carbon Footprint
18-35.description: Connect personal choices to climate impact and explore actionable solutions

en.title: Climate Action and Your Carbon Footprint
en.welcome: Climate change can feel overwhelming, but individual and collective action matter. Understanding your carbon footprint and available solutions helps you contribute meaningfully. Let's explore practical climate action!
en.mainContent:
**Carbon footprint** measures greenhouse gas emissions from your activities, expressed in CO₂-equivalent. Average American: ~16 tons CO₂/year. Global average: ~4 tons. Paris Agreement targets require ~2 tons/person by 2050. Major categories: transportation, housing (heating/cooling/electricity), food, goods/services, and waste.

**Transportation**: Largest footprint for many. Flying is most carbon-intensive per mile. A round-trip transatlantic flight: ~1-2 tons CO₂. Driving averages 0.4 kg CO₂/mile. Public transit, biking, walking, carpooling, and electric vehicles (charged with renewable energy) reduce impact. Remote work eliminates commuting emissions. Aviation alternatives for regional travel: trains emit 10% of flight emissions.

**Housing energy**: Heating/cooling and electricity vary by energy source. Fossil fuel power produces ~0.5-1 kg CO₂/kWh; renewable energy near-zero. Actions: improve insulation, use efficient appliances, install smart thermostats, switch to LED bulbs, choose renewable energy plans where available. Solar panels reduce footprint significantly if feasible.

**Food**: Agriculture produces ~25% of global emissions. Beef has highest footprint (~27 kg CO₂/kg meat) due to methane from cattle and feed production. Plant-based foods: orders of magnitude lower. Reducing meat/dairy consumption significantly cuts footprint. Local food marketing sometimes misleads - transport is small portion of food emissions; production method matters most.

**Consumption**: Manufacturing goods has embedded carbon. Fast fashion, excessive packaging, single-use plastics, and planned obsolescence waste resources and energy. Strategies: buy less, choose durable quality, repair rather than replace, buy used, support circular economy businesses. Each avoided purchase is emissions saved.

**Systemic action**: Individual footprint reduction matters but system change is essential. Supporting climate policy, voting for climate-conscious candidates, divesting from fossil fuels, pressuring corporations, and participating in climate activism amplify individual impact. Individual and systemic action aren't either/or - both necessary.

**Career choices**: Your profession influences climate impact beyond personal footprint. Working in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, climate policy, green building, environmental law, clean technology, or climate communication multiplies impact. Even within non-climate fields, pushing for sustainability creates change.

**Climate anxiety** affects many facing existential threat. Managing it requires balancing awareness with agency. Strategies: focus on controllable actions, engage in collective action for efficacy, limit doomscrolling, celebrate progress, connect with nature, and seek community. Anxiety channeled into action becomes motivation; paralysis helps no one.

**Greenwashing**: Companies making misleading environmental claims. Critical evaluation: Look for specific measurable commitments, third-party verification, transparency about challenges, and substantive changes (not just marketing). Genuine climate leadership includes supply chain emissions (Scope 3), not just direct operations.
keyPoints: Carbon footprint averages 16 tons US, 4 tons globally; Paris targets require ~2 tons by 2050
Transportation and food (especially meat/dairy) are largest controllable footprint sources
Housing energy footprint depends on source; renewable energy and efficiency reduce impact
Consumption reduction through durability, repair, and avoiding fast fashion cuts emissions
Systemic action through policy, voting, and activism amplifies individual impact

en.wisdomMoment: Climate action isn't about perfection or guilt - it's about doing what you can while pushing for systemic change. Your choices matter both directly (emissions reduced) and indirectly (normalizing sustainable behavior, supporting green businesses, demonstrating demand). Perfect is the enemy of good!
en.core_metaphor: Climate action is like steering a large ship - individual efforts turn the wheel while systemic changes provide the power
en.cta: Calculate your carbon footprint using an online calculator. Identify your largest sources. Choose one meaningful reduction action to implement this month!
en.summary: You've explored carbon footprint concept and targets, transportation impacts with alternatives, housing energy depending on source, food production especially meat/dairy, consumption patterns and circular economy, systemic action amplifying individual efforts, career choices multiplying impact, managing climate anxiety through agency, and evaluating greenwashing claims. 36-60.title: Climate, Community, and Legacy
36-60.description: Navigate climate action through parenting, community, and long-term thinking

en.title: Climate, Community, and Legacy
en.welcome: Climate change affects the world you're leaving to the next generation. Your actions, values, and voice shape both immediate impact and long-term legacy. Let's explore meaningful climate engagement!
en.mainContent:
**Parenting through climate change** raises complex questions. How do you discuss climate threats without creating anxiety? How do you maintain hope while acknowledging reality? Balance matters: honest about challenges, emphasizing solutions and agency, modeling productive engagement rather than despair. Climate-aware parenting includes outdoor time fostering nature connection, teaching sustainability skills, supporting climate education, and demonstrating values through choices.

**Home and property** decisions have long-term climate implications. Energy efficiency improvements (insulation, windows, HVAC) reduce emissions and costs. Solar panels increasingly economical in many regions. Heat pumps for heating/cooling more efficient than fossil fuel systems. Choices made now affect decades of emissions. Property values increasingly reflect climate risks (flooding, fire, heat) and sustainability features.

**Community climate action** often feels more impactful than individual efforts. Joining local climate groups, attending city council meetings about sustainability policies, supporting community solar projects, participating in tree planting, advocating for bike lanes and public transit - collective action achieves what individuals can't. Community engagement builds solidarity and efficacy.

**Professional influence** extends beyond your carbon footprint. Pushing for sustainability in your workplace, whether corporate responsibility, supply chain improvements, or operational efficiency, multiplies impact. Board membership, professional associations, and networking provide platforms for climate advocacy. Your professional expertise applied to climate challenges creates leverage.

**Financial choices** matter significantly. Divesting retirement accounts from fossil fuels and investing in sustainable funds shifts capital. Banking with institutions not funding fossil fuel expansion aligns money with values. Supporting B Corporations and sustainable businesses creates market signals. Individual financial choices aggregate into market forces.

**Political engagement**: Voting for climate-conscious candidates at all levels (local elections often matter most for immediate policy). Contacting representatives about climate legislation. Supporting climate ballot initiatives. Donating to environmental organizations or climate-focused candidates. Democracy enables collective decision-making - participating shapes outcomes.

**Grief and eco-anxiety**: Facing climate reality causes legitimate grief for degraded ecosystems, threatened species, and imperiled futures. Processing this grief healthily involves acknowledging loss, connecting with others sharing concerns, taking meaningful action, limiting exposure to overwhelming information, and maintaining hope through progress observation. Therapy or support groups help some people.

**Legacy thinking**: Climate change reframes legacy questions. What world are you helping create? What values are you modeling? What systems are you supporting or challenging? Climate action is intergenerational ethics enacted daily. Small sustained efforts over decades compound significantly.

**Adaptation planning**: Even with mitigation, some climate impacts are unavoidable. Considering climate resilience in decisions matters: property location regarding flood/fire/heat risk, emergency preparedness, community resilience, and supporting vulnerable populations. Adaptation isn't defeatism - it's realism enabling continued functioning.
keyPoints: Climate-aware parenting balances honesty about challenges with emphasis on solutions and agency
Home decisions on efficiency and energy sources affect decades of emissions and costs
Community climate action through local groups and advocacy achieves collective impact
Professional and financial choices multiply individual impact through institutional influence
Legacy thinking reframes daily choices as intergenerational ethics
interactionPrompts: How do you balance climate awareness with maintaining hope?
What community climate action opportunities exist in your area?
en.wisdomMoment: Climate action at this life stage isn't about perfection but about using your influence - as parent, professional, community member, citizen, and consumer - to push systems toward sustainability. Your sustained engagement over decades compounds into significant impact. Legacy isn't what you leave; it's what you're building daily!
en.core_metaphor: Climate action is like tending a garden - consistent care over time creates flourishing
en.cta: Identify one community climate initiative to support. Attend a meeting, volunteer, or advocate. Community action provides efficacy and connection!
en.summary: You've explored climate-aware parenting balancing honesty and hope, home decisions affecting long-term emissions, community action achieving collective impact, professional influence multiplying effects, financial choices shifting capital, political engagement shaping policy, processing grief and eco-anxiety healthily, legacy thinking as intergenerational ethics, and adaptation planning for resilience. Your influence compounds over time!

61-102.title: Climate Across a Lifetime
61-102.description: Reflect on witnessing climate changes and sharing intergenerational wisdom

en.title: Climate Across a Lifetime
en.welcome: You've witnessed climate across many decades - perhaps noticing shifts in seasons, weather extremes, or ecosystem changes. Your long-term perspective is invaluable for understanding what's changing and what remains. Let's reflect on climate across your lifetime.
en.mainContent:
Perhaps you remember weather patterns being different - winters more reliably snowy, springs arriving at different times, summers feeling different, or fewer extreme events. Your memory provides baseline data for change. Scientists call this 'shifting baseline syndrome' - each generation accepts current conditions as normal. Your experience counters this, providing historical context younger people lack.

You've possibly noticed phenological changes - flowers blooming earlier, birds arriving at different times, fall colors peaking at different dates, ice-out on lakes occurring earlier. These seasonal timing shifts, observed consistently over decades, document climate change through biological responses. Your observations are data points in larger patterns.

Perhaps local ecosystems changed visibly - species once common becoming rare, new species appearing that weren't present decades ago, forests stressed by heat or drought, or water bodies behaving differently. These changes you've witnessed firsthand demonstrate climate impacts more tangibly than statistics. Your experience makes climate change real rather than abstract.

You may remember when climate change wasn't widely discussed - before it became politicized, before consensus emerged, when it was purely scientific question. Witnessing the evolution of public understanding, the emergence of denial campaigns, and the growing acceptance provides perspective on how societies process difficult truths. This meta-awareness helps understand current climate discourse.

Your generation's energy consumption grew dramatically across your lifetime - from minimal electricity use to always-on devices, from rare flying to common air travel, from local economies to global supply chains. Witnessing this transition helps understand how current emissions levels developed. It also reveals that major lifestyle changes are possible - society transformed once; it can again.

Perhaps climate change affects you through health (heat sensitivity, air quality affecting breathing), property (values reflecting climate risk, insurance costs rising), or worry about grandchildren inheriting degraded world. These personal impacts make climate change immediate rather than distant future threat.

You might feel complicated emotions - some responsibility for emissions (though systemic factors matter more than individual choices), grief for environmental degradation, frustration at delayed action, hope from growing awareness, and concern for younger generations. These feelings are legitimate and shared by many elders processing climate reality.

Sharing your observations with younger people provides invaluable historical context. What was 'normal' weather/seasons/ecosystems in your youth? What changes have you witnessed? How has public understanding evolved? This inter generational knowledge transfer helps younger people understand the trajectory of change. Your perspective spanning decades is precious data.

You can contribute through: Sharing observations with family and scientists. Supporting climate action within your capacity. Modeling values for grandchildren. Voting for climate-conscious representatives. Donating to environmental causes. Every contribution matters regardless of age. Your voice carries weight of experience.
keyPoints: Decades of memory provide baseline for understanding climate shifts
Phenological observations (seasonal timing) document climate change through biology
Witnessed ecosystem changes make climate impacts tangible rather than abstract
Experience spanning pre-climate discourse to present provides perspective on social processing
Sharing long-term observations with younger generations transfers invaluable historical context
interactionPrompts: What climate or ecosystem changes have you noticed across your lifetime?
What observations or wisdom would you share with younger generations?
en.wisdomMoment: Your lifetime observations of climate and ecosystems are irreplaceable historical records. The changes you've witnessed, the baselines you remember, the transformations you've observed - this lived experience provides context younger generations can't access elsewhere. Sharing this perspective helps society understand climate change trajectory and motivates action. Your memory is valuable climate data!
en.core_metaphor: Your lifetime climate observations are like a living archive spanning generations of change

en.cta: Document your climate observations - what you remember as 'normal', what's changed, what you've witnessed. Share this with family, scientists, or community. Your experience is precious data!
en.summary: You've reflected on remembering different weather patterns providing baseline data, phenological changes documenting climate impacts, ecosystem transformations witnessed firsthand, evolution of climate discourse understanding, lifestyle transformation demonstrating change is possible, personal climate impacts through health and property, complicated emotions processing reality, sharing observations providing historical context, and contributing through voice and action. Your lifetime perspective is invaluable climate wisdom!

es.title: Clima a través de una vida
es.welcome: ¡Has sido testigo del clima a lo largo de muchas décadas!
keyPoints: Décadas de memoria proporcionan línea base para comprender cambios climáticos
interactionPrompts: ¿Qué cambios climáticos o ecosistémicos has notado a lo largo de tu vida?
¿Qué observaciones o sabiduría compartirías con las generaciones más jóvenes?
es.core_metaphor: Tus observaciones climáticas son como un archivo vivo

fr.title: Climat à travers une vie
fr.welcome: Tu as été témoin du climat pendant de nombreuses décennies!
keyPoints: Des décennies de mémoire fournissent une base pour comprendre les changements climatiques
interactionPrompts: Quels changements climatiques ou écosystémiques as-tu remarqués au cours de ta vie?
Quelles observations ou sagesse partagerais-tu avec les jeunes générations?
fr.core_metaphor: Tes observations climatiques sont comme une archive vivante

phases.content: Your long-term climate perspective is invaluable!
Weather patterns, phenology, ecosystems, discourse, and personal impacts across decades!

teachingMoments.explanation: Decades of observation provide irreplaceable historical context
teachingMoments.ageAppropriate: Honoring lived experience as climate data

phases.content: What climate changes have you witnessed?
Your lifetime perspective is invaluable climate wisdom!
Your memory is valuable climate data worth sharing!

scaffolding.shifting_baselines: Each generation accepting current conditions as normal

universal_concepts: Climate is long-term weather patterns; weather is day-to-day conditions
Earth has distinct climate zones from geometry and atmospheric circulation
Climate affects ecosystems, agriculture, and human life
Climate is changing due to human activities; action matters
crossAgeThemes.progression_notes: Moves from weather vs climate distinction (2-5) to climate zones and patterns (6-12) to climate science and data (13-17) to carbon footprint and action (18-35) to community and legacy (36-60) to lifetime observations and intergenerational wisdom (61-102)
